docs.title: RAVEN
docs.text:
Ravens see what you can't.

Documentation for RAVEN (bgp-routing-security-monitor) — BMP + RPKI ROV + ASPA path validation in a single binary.

Route validation is becoming router-native. Visibility into the RPKI infrastructure your router depends on for that validation is not. RAVEN provides that visibility.

RAVEN is an open-source, lightweight, single-binary routing security observability tool. It connects directly to your routers via BMP (BGP Monitoring Protocol) and your RPKI validators via RTR, annotates every route with its security posture in real-time, and exposes the results through a CLI, Prometheus metrics, and Grafana dashboards. Alongside route-level validation, RAVEN also watches the RTR sessions themselves — the link between your router and its RPKI validator — with adaptive anomaly detection on cache sync behavior, independent of whether any individual route ends up flagged.

docs.title: What Does RAVEN Answer?
docs.text:
"Show me every route I'm receiving, whether the origin is RPKI-valid, whether the AS_PATH is ASPA-valid, and what I should do about the ones that aren't."

No existing tool answers this question. BMP collectors don't validate. RPKI validators don't see live routes. External monitors can't see your internal routing state. RAVEN fills that gap.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
# Install
go install github.com/nokia/bgp-routing-security-monitor/cmd/raven@latest

# Start RAVEN — point at your router (BMP) and validator (RTR)
raven serve --config raven.yaml

# In another terminal — see your routes
raven routes --posture origin-invalid

docs.title: Why Now?
docs.text: ASPA has crossed into production availability — ARIN enabled ASPA object creation in January 2026, RIPE NCC in December 2025. Adoption is under 1% of the global ASN space. The tooling gap is a significant barrier. RAVEN is the first operational tool that brings ASPA validation to your live routing table.

docs.title: Beyond Validation
docs.text:
ROV and ASPA validation are becoming router-native. As vendors ship these checks directly in the data plane, the case for an external tool doing route-by-route validation gets weaker over time — that's the correct outcome for the ecosystem.

What doesn't move onto the router is the health of the RPKI infrastructure itself. A router validates against whatever its RTR cache tells it — it has no way to notice that the cache's sync behavior just changed, that VRPs are being withdrawn in a pattern that doesn't match normal churn, or that the cache has started behaving differently from its own history. RAVEN's RTR monitoring and anomaly detection answer a different question than "is this route valid" — they answer "is the thing my router trusts to make that call behaving normally." That's infrastructure-layer observability, and it stays relevant however far ROV/ASPA adoption goes.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to RAVEN are recorded here.

docs.title: Breaking changes
docs.text:
• ROV takes the origin AS as RFC 6811 §2 defines it. A route whose AS_PATH ends in an AS_SET has origin NONE: Invalid if a VRP covers the prefix, NotFound otherwise. Earlier releases used the set's last member, so some aggregates change from Valid to Invalid. Confederation segments never supply the origin.
  • raven validate exits with an error when given --origin-asn or --rtr, which it used to accept and ignore. Remove them from scripts.
  • The HTTP API now binds to 127.0.0.1:11020 by default instead of port 11020 on every interface, and is configurable with the new api.listen key. If you run the CLI from another host with --address, set api.listen on the daemon to a reachable address and firewall it.
  • raven status and the API's route_table.total_routes and by_posture now count Adj-RIB-In pre-policy routes only. Earlier releases added every RIB the routers sent, so routers sending post-policy or Adj-RIB-Out data inflated the totals. Dashboards built on those numbers will show lower, correct values.
  • raven_bmp_peer_state gained the router_addr and peer_distinguisher labels. The same peer address on two routers, or in two VRFs of one router, is now two series.
  • ASPA verification follows draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification-24. The "first-hop" check of the neighbor-to-you edge, which required the neighbor's ASPA record to list your AS, was removed because the draft does not evaluate that edge. A route whose AS_PATH holds only the neighbor's AS now verifies as Valid, and sessions that showed path-suspect on every route because of that check no longer do.
  • Snapshots are written in format_version 2. A snapshot from an earlier release is not restored; RAVEN starts with an empty route table and rebuilds it from the routers' BMP table dumps.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• RFC 7606 error handling for malformed BGP UPDATEs, mirroring the monitored router: attribute discard, treat-as-withdraw and session reset. Withdrawals apply even from malformed UPDATEs. Peers that send a session-reset error show a MALFORMED column in raven peers and malformed_input, malformed_reason and malformed_since in /api/v1/peers. New metric raven_bmp_malformed_updates_total{action,reason}; a WARN log line at most once a minute per peer and reason.
  • raven routes --rib and the rib parameter on /api/v1/routes and /api/v1/watch: list one RIB (default adj-rib-in-pre), with every other filter applied within it.
  • --router on raven status and raven peers. On raven status it limits the peer list; the totals stay daemon-wide.
  • Route JSON timestamp: when the monitored router received the route, from the BMP per-peer header, in RFC 3339 UTC; RAVEN's receive time when the router sends 0.
  • rtr.expire-interval now overrides every cache's Expire Interval, clamped to 600–172800 seconds, and RAVEN logs the interval in effect at startup. Earlier releases parsed the key and never used it.
  • ASPA: routes whose AS_PATH has confederation segments are Unverifiable with an aspa_reason (draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification-24 §6.2).
  • validation.aspa-peers: map a BMP peer, by address or ASN, to its neighbor-role (provider, customer, peer, rs, rs-client). provider selects downstream ASPA verification, every other role upstream. Address entries take precedence over ASN entries; unmapped peers use validation.aspa-default-procedure, which is now honored (auto falls back to upstream until BGP Role parsing exists). Mapped peers other than rs also get the draft's neighbor-AS check.
  • Route JSON gains router, router_name, peer_distinguisher, path_id, aspa_procedure, aspa_procedure_source, aspa_reason and aspa_failing_hop.
  • raven routes --format wide, adding the ASPA PROCEDURE, PROCEDURE SOURCE and FAILING HOP columns. raven routes gains a ROUTER column, and raven routes and raven watch gain --router (router address or BMP sysName).
  • raven status and raven peers gain a ROUTER column and, when any peer has Adj-RIB-Out routes, an OUT column.
  • Routes are keyed by router, peer distinguisher, peer address, prefix, ADD-PATH path ID and RIB type. Two routers with the same peer address, VRF peers with the same address, and ADD-PATH paths no longer overwrite each other. ADD-PATH is negotiated per address family and direction from the Peer Up OPENs.
  • bmp.allowed-routers: accept BMP only from listed addresses and prefixes. Other sources are closed at accept, logged at WARN and counted. With the list empty, RAVEN warns at startup when BMP listens on a non-loopback address.
  • One listeners bound log line at startup with every listener's resolved address. A BMP bind failure now exits non-zero.
  • BMP decoding: Adj-RIB-Out (RFC 8671), IPv4 unicast in MP_REACH_NLRI/MP_UNREACH_NLRI including RFC 8950 IPv6 next hops, per-family ADD-PATH, RFC 9072 extended optional parameters, and AS4_PATH merging for two-octet AS_PATHs. make fuzz runs the FuzzBMPMessage, FuzzPeerUpOpen and FuzzDecodeUpdate targets.
  • Incremental revalidation: an RTR sync revalidates only the routes its VRP and ASPA changes can affect, instead of the whole table.
  • New Prometheus metrics: raven_aspa_validations_total{procedure,source,state}, raven_revalidation_duration_seconds{mode}, raven_revalidation_routes_total{mode,result}, raven_bmp_rejected_connections_total{reason}, raven_adj_rib_out_routes_total{posture,afi} and raven_bmp_unsupported_nlri_total{afi,safi}. Counters and histograms with fixed label sets are exported at 0 from startup.
  • On-demand global BGP visibility correlation via the RIPEstat Data API. RAVEN's ROV/ASPA validation is local-vantage-point only and cannot distinguish a globally propagated hijack from a purely local leak; this compares the local BMP-observed origin for a prefix against the origin ASNs that RIS route collectors see for it. Verdicts are match, divergent, local_only or inconclusive.
  • raven check global --prefix <cidr> [--origin-asn N] [--format table|json] — one-shot correlation showing the local BMP view beside the global view with a consensus verdict. Works without a running daemon when --origin-asn is supplied.
  • New external.ripestat config section (enabled, base-url, timeout, cache-ttl, rate-limit-per-min), defaulting to disabled. Existing raven.yaml files are unaffected without an explicit opt-in.
  • New Event Engine action type global-correlate, configurable per rule with an optional cache_ttl. It runs before the rule's other actions and annotates the event, so webhook payloads gain a global_visibility field and the log action gains global_* keys. Rules that do not use it are unaffected. Correlation runs in the Event Engine's own goroutines behind a per-prefix cache, a token-bucket rate limiter and a concurrency bound — never on the BMP ingest or validation path, and with no per-route external HTTP calls.
  • New Prometheus metrics: raven_global_check_total{source,result}, raven_global_check_latency_seconds, raven_global_check_rate_limited_total{source} and raven_global_check_cache_hits_total{source}. The last two count the lookups that made no network round-trip — suppressed by the local rate limiter, or served from the in-process cache — and are deliberately kept off the latency histogram, which covers live lookups only. A policy decision and a warm cache must both stay distinguishable from a provider RAVEN could not reach.

The result is a standalone annotation: it does not feed into SecurityPosture and the ROV × ASPA posture matrix is unchanged. The whole path is fail-open — an unreachable, slow or malformed RIPEstat degrades to inconclusive and never crashes RAVEN or blocks an action. - Grafana: Global BGP Visibility Correlation dashboard row — consensus results timeseries, current totals stat panel, RIPEstat query performance, and latency p50/p95 panels (panels 17–20). - RTR anomaly detection: adaptive median/MAD-based detector for RTR sync telemetry (interval, duration, VRP/ASPA churn) with per-cache rolling baselines, hard-trip and correlated-trip classification. - Restart-safe baseline persistence via --anomaly-snapshot on raven rtr monitor — anomaly detector windows survive process restarts. - raven rtr seed-baseline command to seed a detector baseline from historical NDJSON telemetry, avoiding the ~25-hour warm-up window on every fresh deployment. - New Prometheus metrics: raven_rtr_anomaly_total, raven_rtr_anomaly_last_timestamp. - lab/04-rtr-anomaly.sh Containerlab demo scenario for live RTR anomaly detection (bulk SLURM ROA injection, serial-based confirmation).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• RAVEN_* environment variable overrides had no effect. They now work for every non-list config key, with dots and dashes mapped to underscores (RAVEN_BMP_LISTEN, RAVEN_RTR_EXPIRE_INTERVAL).
  • A Route Monitoring message with a BGP Length under 19 crashed the daemon.
  • --prefix and --origin-asn on raven routes returned routes from every RIB; every query now returns one RIB.
  • raven routes applied only the first of --prefix, --origin-asn, --peer and --posture; every filter given now applies. raven watch sent only --posture to the daemon; it now sends every filter.
  • Per-peer route counts counted every announced prefix in every UPDATE and never decreased on withdrawal. They now reflect the route table.
  • VRP changes rebuilt the whole VRP index under a write lock for every withdrawn VRP, stalling ROV lookups and BMP ingest (81 minutes for one 8,882-VRP withdrawal in production). VRP changes now publish once at End of Data through an off-lock rebuild and atomic swap, and routes keep validating against the previous VRP set during a full sync.
  • A post-policy withdrawal no longer removes the pre-policy route, and a peer-down on one router no longer removes other routers' routes.
  • A Withdrawn Routes Length longer than the UPDATE crashed the daemon; BMP messages are now capped at 1 MiB.
  • RTR Error Report code 2 ("No Data Available", sent by Routinator during initial validation) is treated as cache-not-ready, not as an anomaly.
  • A raven.yaml that exists but does not parse is now fatal. RAVEN prints the error (naming the offending file) to stderr and exits 1. Previously a YAML syntax error printed one line and then started the daemon anyway on silently-defaulted config — rtr_caches:0, no BMP peers, no event rules, exit 0 — so a single mis-indented key left an operator with a daemon that looked healthy and validated nothing. A missing config file stays non-fatal: RAVEN still runs on defaults when no raven.yaml exists.
  • Global-visibility lookups suppressed by the local rate limiter are no longer reported as queries. The result now carries queried: false and no latency_ns, instead of queried: true with a sub-microsecond latency for a call that never left the process. They are counted on the new raven_global_check_rate_limited_total{source} rather than folded into raven_global_check_total{result="inconclusive"}, and contribute no observation to raven_global_check_latency_seconds, which now describes only real network attempts. In Prometheus and Grafana, "the rate limiter fired" and "RIPEstat was unreachable" are now separate signals.
  • CLI errors are now printed to stderr. The root command sets SilenceErrors, so cobra did not print returned errors and main discarded them — every CLI failure exited 1 with no output at all, including config validation errors and commands' actionable hints.
  • RTR anomaly detector no longer evaluates or contaminates its baseline with full (non-incremental) RTR syncs, which previously produced a false-positive high-severity anomaly on every raven rtr monitor startup.
  • Upstream ASPA verification (internal/validation/aspa) now checks the first hop of the AS_PATH — whether the immediate peer AS lists the monitoring router's own AS as an authorised provider. This check previously stopped one hop short, so a real route-propagation misconfiguration over a peering session without a matching ASPA provider entry resolved as ASPA:Unknown instead of ASPA:Invalid. Single-AS-path routes, previously short-circuited to Unknown with no check at all, are now actually evaluated.
  • Adds LocalASN to Route, learned per BMP session from the Peer Up message's Sent OPEN (RFC 6793 four-octet AS capability preferred when present) via new parseOpenLocalASN() in internal/bmp/parser.go. No config changes needed.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text: • Any direct BGP session where the peer's ASPA record does not list the local AS as a provider now shows path-suspect for every prefix received over that session — not just customer-originated misannouncements, but connected-link and infrastructure prefixes too. docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: This page covers the most common issues encountered when deploying and running RAVEN. These are hard-won lessons from real deployments.

docs.title: Routers Not Connecting
docs.text:
Symptom: raven peers shows no peers. raven status shows BMP listener running but no sessions.

Check 1 — Is the BMP listener actually running?

ss -tlnp | grep 11019

If nothing shows, RAVEN is not listening. Check the logs:

journalctl -u raven -n 50

Check 2 — Can the router reach RAVEN?

From the router, test connectivity to RAVEN's BMP port:

# FRR — test from the router
ping 192.0.2.10
telnet 192.0.2.10 11019

Check 3 — Firewall blocking the connection?

# On the RAVEN host
iptables -L INPUT -n | grep 11019

Check 4 — BMP config on the router correct?

Verify the destination IP and port match RAVEN's listen address exactly. A common mistake is configuring the router's management IP instead of the IP reachable from the router's BGP interfaces.

Check 5 — Is RAVEN rejecting the router?

If you set bmp.allowed-routers, RAVEN closes connections from any other source and logs why:

journalctl -u raven | grep 'BMP connection rejected'

The log line's remote field is the address the router connected from. Routers often source BMP from a loopback rather than the interface facing RAVEN; add that address to bmp.allowed-routers. The raven_bmp_rejected_connections_total{reason="not_allowed"} counter rises with each rejection.

docs.title: Routes Not Appearing
docs.text:
Symptom: raven peers shows a peer UP but raven routes returns nothing or very few routes.

Cause: The BMP table dump is still in progress. After a router connects, it sends a full table dump which can take 30-90 seconds for a full DFZ table.

Check:

# Watch route count grow
watch -n 2 raven status

The route count next to the peer should be increasing. Wait until it stabilises before expecting complete results.

If routes never appear:

Check whether the router is configured to send Adj-RIB-In Pre-Policy. Some router configurations only send Loc-RIB or post-policy by default: FRR — explicitly configure pre-policy bmp targets raven monitor ipv4 unicast pre-policy monitor ipv6 unicast pre-policy exit

docs.title: All Routes Showing as Unverified
docs.text:
Symptom: Every route shows posture unverified. ROV state is NotFound for all routes.

Cause: RAVEN has no VRPs — the RTR session to the validator is not working.

Check:

raven status
curl -s http://localhost:9595/metrics | grep -E 'raven_rtr_(session_state|vrp_count|last_sync_seconds|data_expired)'

raven status shows the VRP count on its RPKI: line. In the metrics, raven_rtr_session_state of 0 means the session to that cache is down, and an old raven_rtr_last_sync_seconds (a Unix timestamp) means syncs have stopped completing.

# Check Routinator is running
curl http://127.0.0.1:8323/api/v1/status

If Routinator is not running:

routinator server &

Wait for it to sync (up to 4 minutes cold start, ~13 seconds warm start).

docs.title: Malformed BGP Input
docs.text:
Symptom: RAVEN logs malformed BGP UPDATE from peer, the raven_bmp_malformed_updates_total counter rises, or raven peers shows a MALFORMED column.

What it means: a peer of your monitored router sent a BGP UPDATE that breaks the BGP encoding rules. Your router handled it under RFC 7606, and RAVEN, which sees the same UPDATE over BMP, handles it the same way. RAVEN applies RFC 7606 so that its route table holds what your router's Adj-RIB-In holds, which is the table RAVEN reports on. Silently dropping a bad UPDATE, as earlier releases did, left routes in RAVEN that the router had already withdrawn; accepting it would store routes with broken attributes.

RFC 7606 sorts errors into three classes, and RAVEN acts on each:

Class (action label) Errors that cause it What RAVEN does attribute_discard A malformed AS4_PATH or AS4_AGGREGATOR (RFC 6793 §6); an attribute that appears more than once Drops the bad attribute and keeps the routes. A discarded AS4_PATH leaves the route with its AS_PATH as sent. Of a repeated attribute, the first copy is kept treat_as_withdraw A malformed or wrongly flagged ORIGIN, AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, MULTI_EXIT_DISC, COMMUNITIES or LARGE_COMMUNITIES; from an internal (iBGP) peer, also LOCAL_PREF, ORIGINATOR_ID or CLUSTER_LIST; an attribute whose length runs past the others; a missing ORIGIN, AS_PATH, or NEXT_HOP for prefixes in the NLRI field Stores none of the UPDATE's routes and withdraws every prefix it announces, so no route with a half-parsed path reaches the table. A truncated AS_PATH never supplies an ROV origin session_reset Length fields that overflow the UPDATE or BGP message; a Withdrawn Routes or NLRI field that cannot be parsed; a malformed MP_REACH_NLRI or MP_UNREACH_NLRI, or either one repeated; an MP_REACH_NLRI next hop of the wrong length; an attribute error in an UPDATE that announces no prefixes (RFC 7606 §5.2) Withdraws every prefix it can still parse and marks the peer as having sent malformed input. Your router resets the BGP session with that peer, and the router's BMP Peer Down then removes the rest of the peer's routes

RAVEN treats a peer as internal when its ASN equals the monitored router's own AS on that BMP session; if RAVEN does not know the router's AS, the peer counts as external.

For session_reset, RAVEN does not close anything itself. The BMP session carries every peer of the router, so closing it would drop all of them over one peer's bad UPDATE.

Withdrawals always apply. Whatever else is wrong with an UPDATE, RAVEN applies the prefixes it withdraws: those in the Withdrawn Routes field whenever RAVEN can find where that field ends, and those in MP_UNREACH_NLRI whenever it can find where the path attributes end. A withdrawal is not lost because another part of its UPDATE was bad. Only when the Withdrawn Routes length itself overflows the UPDATE is there nothing RAVEN can safely withdraw.

Where to see it:

  • raven peers shows a MALFORMED column naming the reason for each peer marked by a session_reset error; see The MALFORMED column. The mark clears when the router reports the peer up again. A peer that stays marked with no Peer Down means your router did not reset that session, and RAVEN's view of the peer may be missing routes.
  • raven_bmp_malformed_updates_total{action, reason} counts every malformed UPDATE, labeled with the strongest class its errors call for and the error that called for it; see Observability & Metrics.
  • A WARN log line, at most one per minute for each peer and reason. Each line's suppressed field counts the ones skipped since the last:
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:44:46.600080233-04:00","level":"WARN","msg":"malformed BGP UPDATE from peer","router_name":"edge1","peer":"198.51.100.1","peer_asn":64500,"peer_distinguisher":"","rib":"adj-rib-in-pre","action":"treat_as_withdraw","reason":"origin","detail":"ORIGIN 03","withdrawals":1,"suppressed":0}

Here peer AS64500 sent an ORIGIN value of 3, which is undefined, so RAVEN treated the UPDATE's one prefix as withdrawn.

What to do: the fault is with the peer, not with RAVEN or your router. Find the peer from the log line's peer and peer_asn, compare with your router's own log of the error, and raise it with the peer's operator. To capture the offending UPDATE for them, run RAVEN with --log-level debug: each malformed UPDATE is then also logged at DEBUG with the whole message in hex (update), as RFC 7606 §6 recommends.

docs.title: Routinator Takes Too Long to Start
docs.text:
Symptom: RAVEN starts but RTR cache shows 0 VRPs for several minutes.

Cause: Routinator is doing a cold start and downloading the full RPKI repository from scratch. This takes approximately 4 minutes.

Solution: Do not kill Routinator between sessions. A warm cache restart takes about 13 seconds. If you must restart, wait for Routinator to fully sync before starting RAVEN.

# Monitor Routinator sync progress
watch -n 5 'curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8323/api/v1/status | python3 -m json.tool'

Wait until vrpsTotal stabilises before proceeding.

docs.title: ASPA Validation Not Working
docs.text:
Symptom: All routes show ASPA state Unknown, and raven_rtr_aspa_count is 0 for every cache:

curl -s http://localhost:9595/metrics | grep raven_rtr_aspa_count

Cause: One of:

  1. Routinator is not started with --enable-aspa
  2. RAVEN negotiated RTR v1 instead of v2
  3. Routinator version does not support ASPA

Check 1 — Routinator ASPA support:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8323/api/v1/status | grep -i aspa

If no ASPA fields appear, restart Routinator with ASPA enabled:

pkill routinator
routinator server --enable-aspa &

Check 2 — RTR version negotiation:

curl -s http://localhost:9595/metrics | grep raven_rtr_protocol_version

If the value is 1, RAVEN is speaking RTR v1 to that cache, which carries no ASPA data. This happens when Routinator was not ready with RTR v2 when RAVEN first connected.

Fix: Restart RAVEN after Routinator is fully synced and running with --enable-aspa. RAVEN will renegotiate RTR v2 on reconnect.

Note

When a cache makes RAVEN downgrade (RTR Error Report code 4), RAVEN re-probes the configured version every rtr.version-reprobe-interval (default 1 hour), so it returns to RTR v2 on its own once the cache supports it. Restart RAVEN if you do not want to wait.

docs.title: RTR Data Keeps Expiring
docs.text:
Symptom: raven_rtr_data_expired goes to 1 repeatedly, or raven_rtr_session_state keeps dropping to 0 as the RTR session drops and reconnects.

Check — Routinator memory:

ps aux | grep routinator

If Routinator is using very high memory or CPU, it may be thrashing during validation. Ensure the host has at least 2GB RAM available for Routinator.

Check — Network connectivity:

nc -zv 127.0.0.1 3323

If this fails, Routinator's RTR listener is not running. Check Routinator logs and restart.

docs.title: Routes Showing as Origin-Invalid Unexpectedly
docs.text:
Symptom: Routes you expect to be valid are showing as origin-invalid.

Cause: Either a misconfigured ROA or a genuine issue.

Investigate:

raven routes --posture origin-invalid --format json | \
  jq '.[] | {prefix, origin_asn, rov_reason}'

rov_reason names the origin AS that no covering VRP authorizes, for example origin AS64502 not authorized by any covering VRP. To see which VRPs cover the prefix, ask your validator. With Routinator:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8323/api/v1/validity/AS64502/203.0.113.0/24

Compare the VRPs it lists against the route's origin_asn and prefix length.

Common causes:

  • ROA authorizes the wrong ASN (misconfiguration at the RIR)
  • ROA maxLength is too restrictive — the route is a more-specific
  • Legitimate route from a secondary origin ASN with no ROA

docs.title: What-If Results Seem Wrong
docs.text:
Symptom: raven what-if --reject-invalid shows 0 routes when you expect some.

Cause: The route table may not be fully loaded yet, or ROV validation has not completed.

Check:

raven status

Confirm route counts are stable and RTR cache has VRPs loaded. Then re-run the what-if simulation.

docs.title: Containerlab Subnet Conflict
docs.text:
Symptom: containerlab deploy fails with subnet conflict error.

Fix: Another Docker network is using 172.20.20.0/24. Find and remove it:

docker network ls
docker network rm <conflicting-network-name>

docs.title: FRR Not Ready After Setup
docs.text:
Symptom: demo-master.sh setup warns that FRR did not become ready.

Fix: The BGP sessions need more time to converge. Wait 30 seconds and check manually:

docker exec clab-raven-demo-upstream vtysh -c "show bgp summary"

Look for the Established state on all peers. If sessions are stuck in Active, check the FRR configs and container connectivity.

docs.title: Prometheus Not Scraping RAVEN
docs.text:
Symptom: Grafana shows no data. Prometheus targets page shows RAVEN as DOWN.

Cause: Common in WSL2 — Prometheus in Docker cannot reach RAVEN on localhost because they are in different network namespaces.

Fix: Use the Docker bridge gateway IP instead of localhost:

ip route | grep default | awk '{print $3}'
# Typically 172.17.0.1

Update your Prometheus scrape config:

static_configs:
  - targets: ["172.17.0.1:9595"]

Restart Prometheus after changing the config.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
If you encounter an issue not covered here:

  1. Check the logs: journalctl -u raven -n 100 or run with --log-level debug
  2. Open an issue on GitHub with your RAVEN version (raven version), config file (redact IPs if needed), and the relevant log output

docs.title: Data Model
docs.text: This page describes how RAVEN turns BMP messages into routes, and how it identifies and stores them. Knowing the route key explains why RAVEN shows the same prefix from the same peer address more than once, and why its counts match what your routers report.

docs.title: From BMP to routes
docs.text:
RAVEN decodes BMP and BGP itself. Its decoder in internal/bmp reads the BMP messages your routers send and the BGP UPDATE and OPEN messages carried inside them. RAVEN does not use GoBGP to parse UPDATEs; GoBGP appears in RAVEN only as the Flowspec injection target for Active Response.

BMP input is untrusted: anything that reaches the BMP port can send it bytes, so the decoder is written to fail safe and is fuzzed. make fuzz in the code repository runs three fuzz targets, FuzzBMPMessage, FuzzPeerUpOpen and FuzzDecodeUpdate, and every failing input found is kept and replayed by the regular test suite. A BMP message longer than 1 MiB closes the session, Statistics Report entries are sized from the bytes present rather than from the count the message claims, and the UPDATE's Withdrawn Routes Length is checked against the message length.

The decoder handles:

  • Peer Up: both the sent and received OPEN messages, including RFC 9072 extended optional parameters. RAVEN reads the ADD-PATH capability from both OPENs to learn, per address family and direction, whether the peer's UPDATEs carry path identifiers.
  • Route Monitoring: withdrawn routes, path attributes and NLRI in the UPDATE body (IPv4 unicast), and MP_REACH_NLRI / MP_UNREACH_NLRI for IPv4 and IPv6 unicast, including IPv6 next hops for IPv4 routes (RFC 8950). Other address families are counted in raven_bmp_unsupported_nlri_total and not stored.
  • AS_PATH: two-octet AS_PATHs, as sent by a peer whose per-peer header has the A flag set, are merged with AS4_PATH (RFC 6793 §4.2.3), so the route carries the real four-octet path.
  • RIB type: the per-peer header tells RAVEN whether a route is Adj-RIB-In pre-policy, Adj-RIB-In post-policy, or Adj-RIB-Out pre- or post-policy (RFC 8671).

A malformed UPDATE is handled the way RFC 7606 tells your router to handle it (attribute discard, treat-as-withdraw or session reset), so RAVEN's table keeps matching the router's Adj-RIB-In; see Malformed BGP Input. Each route also carries the BMP per-peer header's timestamp, the time the router received it.

Routes and withdrawals from all BMP sessions go to the route table over one channel, in the order each router sent them, so a peer-down is never applied before routes from that peer that were still queued.

docs.title: The route
docs.text:
Each route RAVEN stores carries:

Field group Contents Where it was learned The monitored router, the peer distinguisher and peer type from the BMP per-peer header, the peer's address and ASN, the ADD-PATH path ID, the RIB type What was announced Prefix, AS_PATH (flattened, and with its segment types kept for ASPA), ORIGIN, next hop, communities, large communities What RAVEN concluded ROV result, ASPA result (state, procedure, procedure source, failing hop, reason), security posture Bookkeeping Whether the route was restored from a snapshot and not yet confirmed live, and which BMP session owns it

The router is the source address of the router's BMP session. The BMP Initiation sysName, when the router sends one, is kept as a display name: that is what the CLI's ROUTER column and the router_name JSON field show.

docs.title: The route key
docs.text:
A route is identified by six parts:

Part Why it is part of the key Router Two routers can have a peer with the same address, such as the same exchange route server. Without the router in the key, each router's routes overwrote the other's Peer distinguisher A router can have peers with the same address in different VRFs. The BMP per-peer header's Peer Distinguisher (the VRF's route distinguisher, zero for the global instance) keeps them apart Peer address The BGP neighbor the route came from Prefix The announced prefix Path ID With ADD-PATH (RFC 7911), one peer can send several paths for the same prefix. Each path ID is a separate route; without ADD-PATH the path ID is 0 RIB type The same route in Adj-RIB-In pre-policy and post-policy, for example, is two entries, so a post-policy withdrawal does not remove the pre-policy route

The first three parts together identify a peer as one monitored router sees it. RAVEN normalizes IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses to plain IPv4 in the router and peer address, so an IPv4 router or peer is one peer however its address arrived.

Withdrawals carry the same six parts, so a withdrawal removes exactly the route it names.

docs.title: The route table
docs.text:
The route table is in memory. Routes live in a 256-shard map keyed by the route key, so lookups and updates for different routes rarely contend for the same lock. Beside it RAVEN keeps:

  • a prefix index (a BART trie), which answers exact-prefix queries and finds every route at or more specific than a prefix, as revalidation needs;
  • an origin-ASN index;
  • a posture index, holding Adj-RIB-In pre-policy routes only;
  • per-peer route counts by RIB type, updated where routes are added and removed, which feed raven status, raven peers and the OpenTelemetry gauges.

Counts that RAVEN reports as "routes" (the route-table total and posture breakdown in raven status, ROUTES in raven peers, raven_routes_total and raven_route_table_size) are Adj-RIB-In pre-policy: what your routers received from their peers before import policy, comparable to the received-routes count on the router. Adj-RIB-Out routes are counted separately, in the OUT column and in raven_adj_rib_out_routes_total, so received and sent routes never add up into one number.

docs.title: Snapshots
docs.text: With persistence enabled, RAVEN writes the route table to a snapshot and restores it at startup, marking restored routes stale until a live BMP message confirms them. Snapshots use format_version 2, which stores the full route key. A snapshot from an older RAVEN, keyed without router, peer distinguisher and path ID, is not restored: RAVEN starts with an empty route table and rebuilds it from the routers' BMP table dumps.

docs.title: Validation Engine
docs.text: The validation engine annotates every route with an ROV result, an ASPA result and a security posture, and keeps those annotations current as your RPKI data changes. This page explains how it does both without stalling BMP ingest.

docs.title: Validating a route
docs.text:
RAVEN validates each route once on ingest:

  1. ROV (RFC 6811): RAVEN looks up the VRPs covering the route's prefix and compares the origin AS and prefix length against them, giving Valid, Invalid or NotFound.
  2. ASPA: RAVEN picks the verification procedure from the peer the route came from (an aspa-peers entry by address, then by ASN, then aspa-default-procedure) and verifies the AS_PATH as described in ASPA Path Verification. Picking the procedure costs two map lookups and no allocations; RAVEN builds the lookup tables once at startup.
  3. Posture: RAVEN combines the two results into one of the security postures.

docs.title: The origin AS
docs.text:
ROV compares VRPs against the route's origin AS, and RFC 6811 §2 defines which AS that is. RAVEN follows it:

AS_PATH ends in Origin ROV result An AS_SEQUENCE The last AS of that sequence Compared against the covering VRPs as usual An AS_SET NONE, which no VRP can match Invalid if any VRP covers the prefix, NotFound otherwise A confederation segment (AS_CONFED_SEQUENCE or AS_CONFED_SET) The route originated inside your router's own AS confederation NotFound Nothing (empty AS_PATH) None NotFound

Confederation segments never supply the origin, wherever they appear: a path with a confederation segment followed by an AS_SEQUENCE takes its origin from the sequence. When the path ends in a confederation segment, RFC 6811 makes the origin your router's own AS, but the BMP session only tells RAVEN the member AS, not the confederation's AS, so RAVEN reports no origin.

An AS_SET hides which of its members originated the route, so a VRP can never confirm it. Earlier releases took the set's last member as the origin, which let a VRP for that AS mark an aggregate Valid. In each case without an origin, origin_asn is 0, the CLI shows -, and rov_reason says why, for example (from RAVEN's validator, on a route 64500 {64502 64503} under a VRP for 203.0.113.0/24):

origin is NONE: AS_PATH ends in an AS_SET (RFC 6811 §2), which no covering VRP can match

docs.title: Routes RAVEN does not ASPA-verify
docs.text:
Two kinds of route get ASPA state Unverifiable with an aspa_reason instead of a verified result:

  • Routes from inside an AS confederation. A route whose AS_PATH has a confederation segment came over an eBGP session between members of your own confederation: routers strip those segments before a route leaves the confederation (RFC 5065). draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification-24 §6.2 says ASPA verification is not recommended on those sessions, and verifying the path anyway would treat member ASes as hops. The reason reads not ASPA-verified: learned over a session internal to an AS confederation (draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification-24 §6.2).
  • Adj-RIB-Out routes (below).

A route whose AS_PATH contains an AS_SET is also Unverifiable, because an AS_SET has no single order to walk.

docs.title: Adj-RIB-Out routes
docs.text: Adj-RIB-Out routes, the routes your router sends rather than receives, get ROV only. ASPA verification is defined for routes received from a neighbor, by that neighbor's relationship to you, so RAVEN marks their ASPA state Unverifiable with a reason saying why. The Event Engine does not evaluate Adj-RIB-Out routes.

docs.title: VRP lookups
docs.text: RAVEN keeps VRPs in a longest-prefix-match index (a BART trie). For each VRP prefix the index holds the list of VRPs covering it, built once and shared by every lookup, so finding the VRPs for a route takes no lock and allocates nothing.

docs.title: Changes publish at End of Data
docs.text:
The RTR client applies a sync's VRP announcements and withdrawals to a working set as the PDUs arrive. Lookups do not see that working set. When the cache sends End of Data, RAVEN rebuilds the index from the working set off to the side, outside any lock, and swaps the new index in atomically.

This follows RTR's model (RFC 8210): a sync is complete at End of Data, and until then the previous data set is the valid one. It has two practical effects:

  • Lookups never wait for a sync. Earlier releases rebuilt the whole index under the write lock for every withdrawn VRP, which blocked ROV lookups and therefore BMP ingest. One large withdrawal held ingest for over an hour in production; RAVEN now does one rebuild per sync.
  • Routes never see a half-applied sync. At the start of a full sync, clearing the working set no longer empties lookups. Routes keep validating against the previous VRP set until End of Data instead of briefly reading NotFound.

docs.title: Incremental revalidation
docs.text:
When an RTR sync changes the VRP or ASPA data, some routes' results change. Revalidating the whole table after every serial change is expensive on a full table, and a typical delta changes only tens of VRPs, so RAVEN revalidates only the routes a change can affect.

For each Cache Response, the RTR client records a delta: the VRPs announced and withdrawn, and the customer ASNs whose ASPA record was added, removed or changed. RAVEN then picks candidate routes from it:

  • ROV candidates: routes whose prefix is at or more specific than the prefix of a changed VRP, found through the route table's prefix trie. Only those routes can be covered by the changed VRP.
  • ASPA candidates: routes whose AS_PATH contains a changed customer ASN, found by scanning the table shard by shard. RAVEN runs this scan only when the delta has ASPA changes.

A delta that changes nothing triggers no work. Some syncs carry no usable delta: a Cache Reset, a Reset Query, a new RTR session or a session-ID change replaces the data wholesale, so RAVEN revalidates every route (a full pass).

Revalidation runs inside the ingest loop, between chunks of BMP work, so the route table keeps a single writer and ingest keeps flowing during a pass. A route whose results did not change is left as it is; RAVEN copies and replaces only the routes whose ROV, ASPA or posture changed. A property test in the code repository checks that an incremental pass always reaches the same results as a full pass.

Each pass logs re-validation complete with its mode (incremental or full), candidates, checked, changed and took, and records raven_revalidation_duration_seconds and raven_revalidation_routes_total (see Observability & Metrics).

docs.title: Deployment Hardening
docs.text:
RAVEN opens up to four listeners: BMP for your routers, the HTTP API for the CLI, the Prometheus metrics endpoint and, when you enable it, pprof. None of them authenticates its clients, so who can reach each port is your access control. This page explains what each listener exposes and how to restrict it.

Start by checking what RAVEN actually bound. At startup it logs one listeners bound line with the resolved address of each listener. With the defaults and no allowed-routers, you see:

{"time":"2026-10-18T22:19:48.267905655-04:00","level":"WARN","msg":"BMP listener accepts connections from any source on a non-loopback address; set bmp.allowed-routers to the routers' addresses","subsystem":"bmp","addr":"[::]:11019"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T22:19:48.268150928-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"listeners bound","bmp":"[::]:11019","api":"127.0.0.1:11020","metrics":"[::]:9595"}

An address of [::] or 0.0.0.0 means every interface. Here BMP and metrics are open to anything that can route to the host, and the API is loopback only.

docs.title: Restrict BMP sources
docs.text:
Anything that can open a TCP connection to the BMP port can feed routes into your route table, change every posture and metric RAVEN reports, and make it parse attacker-chosen input. An internet scanner found an exposed BMP port on a production RAVEN deployment within a day. Restrict BMP in two places.

1. Set bmp.allowed-routers to your routers' BMP source addresses:

bmp:
  listen: ":11019"
  allowed-routers:
    - 192.0.2.10              # edge1
    - 192.0.2.11              # edge2
    - 2001:db8:100::/64       # core routers' loopbacks

RAVEN closes a connection from any other source at accept, before it reads anything or starts a TLS handshake, logs BMP connection rejected: source not in bmp.allowed-routers at WARN, and counts it in raven_bmp_rejected_connections_total{reason="not_allowed"}. Alert on that counter: see the RAVENBMPRejectedConnection rule in Observability & Metrics.

Use the address the router sources BMP from, which is often its loopback rather than the interface facing RAVEN. If the router's sessions do not appear after you set the list, look for the rejection WARN: it names the address the router connected from.

With allowed-routers empty, RAVEN accepts any source and logs a WARN at startup when the BMP listener is not on loopback. Treat that WARN as a finding.

2. Filter the port in the host firewall as well. The allowlist protects RAVEN; the firewall keeps the port closed to everyone else, keeps connection attempts out of RAVEN's logs, and still holds if someone empties the list in a config change. With nftables, for example:

table inet raven {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority 0; policy accept;
    tcp dport 11019 ip saddr { 192.0.2.10, 192.0.2.11 } accept
    tcp dport 11019 ip6 saddr 2001:db8:100::/64 accept
    tcp dport 11019 drop
  }
}

If your routers support it, BMP over TLS with a client CA adds router authentication on top.

docs.title: Keep the API on loopback
docs.text:
The HTTP API serves the CLI: the full route table, every peer, and the what-if, audit and Flowspec endpoints, including POST /api/v1/flowspec/rules/<key>/toggle-dryrun, which switches a Flowspec rule from dry-run to live injection. It has no authentication. By default it binds to 127.0.0.1:11020, so only users with a shell on the monitoring host can use it.

Keep that default and run the CLI on the monitoring host. If you need the CLI elsewhere, prefer an SSH tunnel to opening the port. Open the tunnel in the background, then run the CLI against your local end of it:

ssh -f -N -L 11020:127.0.0.1:11020 raven-host.example.net

raven routes --posture origin-invalid

If you do set api.listen to a routable address, bind it to a management interface and firewall it to the hosts that run the CLI, as for BMP above. See api.listen.

docs.title: Decide who may scrape metrics
docs.text:
The metrics endpoint (outputs.prometheus.listen, default :9595) binds to every interface. Metrics carry your routers' names and addresses, every BGP peer's address, your RPKI caches' addresses, and route counts by posture, which tells a reader how many of your routes fail validation. That is reconnaissance value, so decide who needs it:

  • If Prometheus runs on the same host, bind metrics to loopback: listen: "127.0.0.1:9595".
  • Otherwise bind it to the management interface and firewall it to your Prometheus servers.

docs.title: pprof stays on loopback
docs.text: The pprof endpoint (debug.pprof.listen) is off by default. When you enable it for a memory investigation, bind it to loopback, for example localhost:6060, and reach it through an SSH tunnel. Profiles reveal process memory contents, and the endpoint is unauthenticated. RAVEN does not stop you binding it elsewhere, but it logs a WARN (pprof endpoint is exposed beyond localhost) when the bound address is not loopback. Turn pprof off again when you are done. See Memory Profiling.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text: Listener Setting Default Recommended BMP bmp.listen, bmp.allowed-routers :11019, any source Your routers only, by allowlist and host firewall API api.listen 127.0.0.1:11020 Loopback; SSH tunnel for remote CLI use Metrics outputs.prometheus.listen :9595 Loopback or management interface, firewalled to Prometheus pprof debug.pprof.listen off Off; loopback only while profiling

docs.title: Production Setup
docs.text: This guide covers deploying RAVEN in a production environment against real routers and a production RPKI validator.

docs.title: Step 1 — Install RAVEN
docs.text:
On the monitoring host:

go install github.com/nokia/bgp-routing-security-monitor/cmd/raven@latest

Or download a pre-built binary from the releases page and place it in /usr/local/bin/.

docs.title: Step 2 — Create the Config File
docs.text:
sudo mkdir -p /etc/raven

Create /etc/raven/raven.yaml:

bmp:
  listen: "0.0.0.0:11019"
  allowed-routers:                  # your routers' BMP source addresses
    - 192.0.2.10
    - 192.0.2.11

rtr:
  caches:
    - address: "rpki-validator.example.com:3323"
      preference: 1
    - address: "rpki-validator-backup.example.com:3323"
      preference: 2
  rtr-version: auto

validation:
  rov: true
  aspa: true
  aspa-default-procedure: upstream
  aspa-peers:                       # map your transit providers
    - address: 198.51.100.1
      neighbor-role: provider

outputs:
  prometheus:
    listen: "0.0.0.0:9595"          # firewall to your Prometheus servers
    path: "/metrics"

api:
  listen: "127.0.0.1:11020"         # the default; run the CLI on this host

logging:
  level: info
  format: json

Before you start RAVEN, work through Deployment Hardening: it covers the host firewall rules for the BMP and metrics ports and how to reach the API from another machine.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: RAVEN is designed as a single-binary, single-instance tool for most deployments. This page covers capacity planning and multi-instance patterns for larger environments.

docs.title: Single Instance Capacity
docs.text:
A single RAVEN instance on modest hardware handles:

Scenario Routes RAM CPU Small network, 1-2 routers, partial table ~100K routes ~512MB minimal Medium network, 5 routers, full DFZ ~5M routes ~4GB 1-2 cores Large network, 10+ routers, full DFZ per router ~120M routes ~16GB 4 cores

The memory target for a full-table multi-router deployment is under 16GB RSS. RAVEN uses a compressed prefix trie (BART) for memory-efficient route storage.

docs.title: Sizing Guidelines
docs.text:
RAM: The dominant factor is the number of routes in the Route Table. Each route object is approximately 512 bytes. Budget 1GB RAM per 1M routes, plus 2GB baseline for the RPKI cache and process overhead.

CPU: RAVEN is designed for high throughput on the BMP ingestion hot path. During initial table dump (when routers first connect), CPU usage spikes briefly then settles to near-zero for steady-state operation. Use 4 cores for large deployments.

Network: BMP is TCP — kernel flow control handles backpressure naturally. No special network sizing needed beyond reliable connectivity between routers and the RAVEN host.

Disk: RAVEN is stateless by default — no disk I/O in steady state. If you enable file output (NDJSON logging), size accordingly.

docs.title: Reducing Memory Usage
docs.text:
If you do not need full pre-policy visibility, configure your routers to send only post-policy BMP: FRR — post-policy only bmp targets raven monitor ipv4 unicast post-policy monitor ipv6 unicast post-policy exit

Post-policy tables are significantly smaller than pre-policy since import policies filter out many routes before installation.

docs.title: Multiple Routers, Single RAVEN Instance
docs.text:
The recommended pattern for most networks — one RAVEN instance receiving BMP from all your routers: Router 1 ──BMP──┐ Router 2 ──BMP──┼──▶ RAVEN ──▶ Prometheus ──▶ Grafana Router 3 ──BMP──┘

RAVEN handles concurrent BMP sessions with one goroutine per session. There is no practical limit on the number of BMP sessions a single instance can accept beyond the RAM budget for the combined route table.

docs.title: Filtering at the Router
docs.text:
For very large deployments, reduce the route table size by filtering BMP exports at the router: FRR — only send routes from specific peers bmp targets raven monitor ipv4 unicast pre-policy neighbor 192.0.2.1 bmp neighbor 192.0.2.2 bmp exit

This is useful when you want to focus RAVEN on specific peering sessions rather than your full BGP table.

docs.title: High Availability
docs.text:
RAVEN is a passive observability tool — it has no role in the data plane. A RAVEN outage does not affect routing. Design for availability based on your monitoring SLA, not routing resilience requirements.

Simple HA pattern — two independent instances: Router 1 ──BMP──▶ RAVEN-1 ──▶ Prometheus-1 Router 2 ──BMP──▶ RAVEN-2 ──▶ Prometheus-2

Run two RAVEN instances receiving from different sets of routers. Aggregate in Prometheus using federation or a shared remote write target. This gives you redundancy without coordination complexity.

Full redundancy — all routers to both instances: ┌──▶ RAVEN-1 ──▶ Prometheus Router 1 ──BMP───┤ └──▶ RAVEN-2 ──▶ Prometheus

Both instances receive the full route table independently. Prometheus aggregates via federation. Use different job labels to distinguish instances. Metrics will be duplicated — use max() or avg() in your PromQL queries rather than sum().

docs.title: Multiple RTR Caches
docs.text:
Always configure a backup RTR cache:

rtr:
  caches:
    - address: "routinator-primary.example.com:3323"
      preference: 1
    - address: "routinator-backup.example.com:3323"
      preference: 2

If the primary cache goes down, RAVEN automatically fails over to the backup and logs a warning. The raven_rtr_session_state metric will show 0 for the failed cache — alert on this.

docs.title: RTR Data Freshness
docs.text:
RAVEN keeps validating with the last data a cache sent, even when that cache stops syncing. Stale RPKI data validates routes against ROAs and ASPA records that may since have changed, so alert on freshness rather than only on the session state. Three per-cache metrics cover it:

Metric What it tells you raven_rtr_data_expired 1 when no sync with the cache has completed within its Expire Interval, the time the cache says its data stays usable. RAVEN takes it from the cache's End of Data PDU, or uses 7200 seconds when the cache sends none raven_rtr_last_sync_seconds Unix time of the last completed sync (End of Data), whether or not the data changed raven_rtr_last_serial_change_seconds Unix time of the last sync that changed the serial 
- alert: RAVENRTRDataExpired
  expr: raven_rtr_data_expired == 1
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: critical
  annotations:
    summary: "RAVEN RTR data has expired — validation data may be outdated"

- alert: RAVENRTRNoRecentSync
  expr: time() - raven_rtr_last_sync_seconds > 1800
  for: 5m
  labels:
    severity: warning
  annotations:
    summary: "No completed RTR sync with {{ $labels.cache }} in 30 minutes"

raven_rtr_data_expired follows the cache's own Expire Interval, so it fires late by design. The second rule catches a cache that stopped syncing well before then; set its threshold to a few multiples of your cache's refresh interval.

docs.title: Querying a Remote RAVEN Instance
docs.text:
The RAVEN CLI can query any RAVEN instance whose API it can reach. The API binds to loopback by default, so either open an SSH tunnel to the instance or set api.listen on it to a management address and firewall that port (see Deployment Hardening). Then:

raven routes --address 192.0.2.10:11020 --posture origin-invalid
raven status --address 192.0.2.10:11020
raven what-if --address 192.0.2.10:11020 --reject-invalid

This is useful for operations teams who want CLI access without running a local RAVEN instance.

docs.title: Prometheus Federation
docs.text:
When running multiple RAVEN instances, aggregate metrics via Prometheus federation:

# Central Prometheus
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: raven-federation
    honor_labels: true
    metrics_path: /federate
    params:
      match[]:
        - '{job="raven"}'
    static_configs:
      - targets:
          - "prometheus-1.example.com:9090"
          - "prometheus-2.example.com:9090"

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: This page explains the core technologies RAVEN builds on. If you're already familiar with BMP, RPKI, and ASPA, skip ahead to the Quick Start.

docs.title: BMP — BGP Monitoring Protocol
docs.text:
BMP (RFC 7854) is a protocol that lets routers stream their BGP routing tables to a monitoring station in real time. Think of it as a live feed of everything your router is receiving from its BGP peers — before and after your import policies are applied.

RAVEN acts as a BMP monitoring station. Your routers connect to RAVEN's BMP listener and send a full table dump on startup, followed by incremental updates as routes change. RAVEN sees every route your router receives, from every peer, in real time.

Why Adj-RIB-In Pre-Policy? RAVEN focuses on Adj-RIB-In Pre-Policy — what the router received before import policy filtered it. This is where security analysis belongs. If a hijacked route is being received and your import policy isn't filtering it, you want to know.

docs.title: RPKI — Resource Public Key Infrastructure
docs.text:
RPKI is a cryptographic framework that allows IP address holders to publish signed records stating which ASNs are authorised to originate their prefixes. These records are called ROAs (Route Origin Authorizations).

Validators like Routinator download and verify ROAs from the five RIRs (ARIN, RIPE NCC, APNIC, LACNIC, AFRINIC) and make the validated data available to routers and tools via the RTR protocol.

docs.title: ROV — Route Origin Validation
docs.text:
ROV (RFC 6811) is the process of checking a received BGP route against the RPKI data. For each route, RAVEN checks:

  • Does any ROA cover this prefix?
  • If yes, does the ROA authorise the origin ASN?
  • Is the prefix length within the ROA's maxLength?

The result is one of three states:

State Meaning Valid A ROA exists that authorises this origin ASN for this prefix Invalid A ROA exists but it does not authorise this origin ASN, or the prefix is too specific NotFound No ROA covers this prefix — no RPKI data available

The origin ASN is the last AS of the AS_PATH. When the path ends in an AS_SET, as an aggregate's can, RFC 6811 says the origin is NONE, which no ROA authorises: RAVEN marks such a route Invalid if a ROA covers the prefix and NotFound otherwise. See The origin AS for every case.

ROV catches origin hijacks — where an attacker announces your prefix from their own ASN. If you have a ROA, the attacker's announcement will be Invalid.

What ROV cannot catch: Route leaks — where a legitimate ASN accidentally re-announces routes they should not. The origin ASN is correct, so ROV passes. This is where ASPA comes in.

docs.title: ASPA — AS Provider Authorization
docs.text:
ASPA (AS Provider Authorization) is a newer RPKI object type that lets an ASN publish which other ASNs are its upstream providers. This creates a signed, verifiable map of customer-provider relationships across the internet.

ARIN enabled ASPA object creation in January 2026. RIPE NCC in December 2025. Adoption is under 1% of the global ASN space today — but growing.

RAVEN is the first operational tool that validates ASPA against your live routing table via BMP.

docs.title: ASPA Path Verification
docs.text: RAVEN verifies AS_PATHs as specified in draft-ietf-sidrops-aspa-verification-24. A route leak occurs when an AS re-announces a route in the wrong direction, for example a customer passing one provider's routes to another provider. The leaked route's AS_PATH then contains a hop where an AS sends a route "up" to an AS that is not its provider, and ASPA records let RAVEN spot that hop.

docs.title: What gets checked
docs.text:
RAVEN collapses prepends, then walks the AS_PATH from the origin to the neighbor, the AS your router learned the route from. For each pair of adjacent ASes it asks the customer AS's ASPA record one question: is the next AS one of my providers? Each hop gets one of three answers:

Hop answer Meaning Provider+ The customer has an ASPA record and it lists the next AS Not Provider+ The customer has an ASPA record and it does not list the next AS No Attestation The customer has no ASPA record

The edge between the neighbor and your router is not checked. Your relationship with the neighbor is what selects the verification procedure (below), so checking that edge again against an ASPA record would test something you already told RAVEN. RAVEN does not need your router's own AS for verification.

That does not leave your attached sessions blind. When a neighbor leaks, it passes on a route it learned from one of its own providers, and that provider-to-neighbor hop is already in the path. Suppose your customer AS64500 leaks a route it received from its provider AS64501:

AS_PATH as your router receives it:  64500 64501 64502
Walked from the origin:              64502 → 64501 → 64500
                                                    ^ AS64501's ASPA does not list AS64500

If AS64501 has published an ASPA record, it does not list its own customer AS64500 as a provider, so that hop is Not Provider+ and the route is Invalid. A route whose AS_PATH holds only the neighbor's AS has no hops to walk and always verifies as Valid: an origin announcing its own prefix to you is not a leak.

docs.title: Upstream and downstream verification
docs.text:
The draft defines two procedures, and which one applies depends on where the route came from:

  • Upstream (§5.4) is for routes from a customer, a lateral peer, a route server or a route-server client. Such a route must have travelled only "up", customer to provider, from the origin to your neighbor. Any Not Provider+ hop makes it Invalid.
  • Downstream (§5.5) is for routes from a provider. A legitimate route from a provider may climb up to a top-tier AS and then come back down toward you, so the path is allowed one up-ramp followed by one down-ramp. It is Invalid only when no such up-then-down split fits the ASPA records.

Using the wrong procedure gives the wrong answer. Verify a provider's routes with the upstream procedure and ordinary transit routes that came down to you look like leaks.

docs.title: How RAVEN chooses the procedure
docs.text:
RAVEN picks the procedure for each route from the BMP peer it was learned from, in this order:

  1. A validation.aspa-peers entry for the peer's address.
  2. A validation.aspa-peers entry for the peer's ASN.
  3. validation.aspa-default-procedure.

An aspa-peers entry names the neighbor's role: provider selects downstream; customer, peer, rs and rs-client select upstream. The default procedure auto falls back to upstream today, because RAVEN does not yet read the BGP Role capability (RFC 9234) that would tell it each neighbor's role. Every route reports the procedure it got and where it came from in aspa_procedure and aspa_procedure_source; see raven routes --format wide.

docs.title: The neighbor-AS check
docs.text:
When a peer's role comes from an aspa-peers entry, RAVEN also runs the draft's neighbor-AS check (§5.4 and §5.5, step 2): the first AS in the AS_PATH must be the peer's own ASN. A route that fails it is Invalid with aspa_reason set, for example:

neighbor-AS check failed: first AS in AS_PATH is AS64511, peer is AS64500

RAVEN skips the check for routes that use the default procedure, because nothing tells it what the neighbor is. It also skips it for rs peers. A route server is transparent: it passes on its clients' routes without adding its own AS to the AS_PATH (RFC 7947), so the first AS is the client that announced the route, never the route server's ASN. Running the check there would mark every route from the route server Invalid.

docs.title: Result states
docs.text:
State Meaning Valid The ASPA records attest the whole path from the origin to your neighbor Invalid A published ASPA record contradicts the path under the selected procedure, or the neighbor-AS check failed: a likely route leak Unknown No record contradicts the path, but some ASes in it have no ASPA record, so RAVEN cannot confirm it. Routes with an empty AS_PATH are also Unknown Unverifiable The AS_PATH contains an AS_SET, so it has no single order to verify, or confederation segments, meaning the route came from inside your own AS confederation, where the draft does not recommend verification (§6.2)

ASPA adoption is early, so expect most of your routes to show Unknown. That changes as more operators publish ASPA records.

docs.title: IPv6 Support
docs.text:
RAVEN monitors IPv6 routes alongside IPv4. BMP messages carrying IPv6 prefixes use the BGP multiprotocol path attributes MP_REACH_NLRI and MP_UNREACH_NLRI (RFC 4760), which RAVEN parses natively for both announcements and withdrawals. Validation runs the same code path as for IPv4 — ROV looks up each IPv6 route against the IPv6 VRP store, and ASPA walks the AS_PATH regardless of the address family.

The CLI exposes IPv6 routes through the same commands as IPv4 (raven routes --prefix 2001:db8::/32 queries an IPv6 prefix), and Prometheus metrics carry an afi="ipv6" label so IPv4 and IPv6 postures can be charted side by side in Grafana.

docs.title: RTR — Router to Relying Party Protocol
docs.text:
RTR (RFC 8210, and RTR v2 in draft-ietf-sidrops-8210bis) is the protocol validators use to deliver VRPs (Validated ROA Payloads) and ASPA data to relying parties. RAVEN maintains a persistent RTR session to your validator and keeps a local copy of all VRP and ASPA data, updated incrementally as the validator's data changes.

RTR v2 adds ASPA PDU support. Routinator with --enable-aspa speaks RTR v2.

docs.title: The Security Posture Model
docs.text: RAVEN combines ROV and ASPA results into a single security posture per route. See Security Postures for the full matrix and operator guidance for each state.

docs.title: What RAVEN Is Not
docs.text:
• Not a router — RAVEN makes no changes to your routing table
  • Not an RPKI validator — it connects to your existing validator via RTR
  • Not an external monitor — it connects to your routers, not public route collectors
  • Not a replacement for BGPalerter — BGPalerter watches from outside, RAVEN watches from inside. Run both.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: RAVEN is a single binary with no runtime dependencies. Pick the method that suits you.

docs.title: Go Install
docs.text:
If you have Go 1.24+ installed:

go install github.com/nokia/bgp-routing-security-monitor/cmd/raven@latest

Verify:

raven version

docs.text:
Download the latest binary for your platform from the GitHub releases page.

chmod +x raven
sudo mv raven /usr/local/bin/

docs.text:

cd bgp-routing-security-monitor

sudo mv raven /usr/local/bin/

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Requirement Details Routers Any BMP-capable router — SR Linux, SR OS, Junos, IOS-XR, Arista EOS, FRR RPKI Validator Any RTR-speaking validator — Routinator, rpki-client, FORT ASPA Routinator with --enable-aspa for RTR v2 + ASPA PDU support Ports BMP listener: 11019/tcp, API: 11020/tcp, Prometheus: 9595/tcp

docs.title: RPKI Validator Setup
docs.text:
RAVEN consumes VRP and ASPA data from your existing RPKI validator via RTR. It does not replace your validator — it connects to it.

For ASPA support, you need Routinator with RTR v2 enabled:

routinator server --enable-aspa --rtr 127.0.0.1:3323

Note

Routinator takes approximately 4 minutes for a cold start while it syncs the RPKI repository. Subsequent starts use a warm cache and take around 13 seconds. Do not restart Routinator unnecessarily.

docs.title: Verify Installation
docs.text:
raven version

Expected output: raven version v0.1.0 (commit: abc1234, built: 2026-04-15T00:00:00Z)

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: This guide gets you from zero to seeing your first annotated routes in minutes.

docs.title: What You Need
docs.text:
• RAVEN binary installed (see Installation)
  • At least one BMP-capable router
  • An RPKI validator running RTR (Routinator recommended)

docs.title: Step 1 — Create a Config File
docs.text:
Create raven.yaml in your working directory:

bmp:
  listen: ":11019"

rtr:
  caches:
    - address: "localhost:3323"
      preference: 1

validation:
  rov: true
  aspa: true

outputs:
  prometheus:
    listen: ":9595"
    path: "/metrics"

logging:
  level: info
  format: json

docs.title: Step 2 — Start RAVEN
docs.text:
raven serve --config raven.yaml

RAVEN logs one JSON object per line. With the config above and Routinator still running its first validation, startup looks like this:

{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.681202942-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"starting raven","version":"dev","commit":"unknown"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.698781115-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"BMP listener started","subsystem":"bmp","addr":"[::]:11019","transport":"tcp","allowed_routers":0}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.699037906-04:00","level":"WARN","msg":"BMP listener accepts connections from any source on a non-loopback address; set bmp.allowed-routers to the routers' addresses","subsystem":"bmp","addr":"[::]:11019"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.6997368-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"listeners bound","bmp":"[::]:11019","api":"127.0.0.1:11020","metrics":"[::]:9595"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.700023699-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"starting RTR clients","count":1}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.700688488-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"RTR expire interval: each cache's own (End of Data)","expire_interval":"cache"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.701255669-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"RAVEN started","bmp_listen":":11019","rtr_caches":1,"rov_enabled":true}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.700086153-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"route ingest pipeline started"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.702104253-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"waiting for RTR sync before annotating routes..."}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.700281373-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"Prometheus metrics endpoint started","addr":"[::]:9595","path":"/metrics"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.702509219-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"API server started","subsystem":"api","addr":"127.0.0.1:11020"}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.705207585-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"RTR connected","subsystem":"rtr","cache":"localhost:3323","transport":"tcp","protocol_version":2}
{"time":"2026-10-18T23:53:32.706773811-04:00","level":"INFO","msg":"RTR cache not ready, reconnecting","subsystem":"rtr","cache":"localhost:3323","error":"cache has no data available yet (Running initial validation)","retry_in":5000000000,"protocol_version":2}

What to look for:

  • listeners bound shows the address each listener bound. The API is on loopback by default.
  • The WARN about bmp.allowed-routers is expected in a first test. Set bmp.allowed-routers before you run RAVEN anywhere a stranger can reach the BMP port; see Deployment Hardening.
  • RTR cache not ready, reconnecting means Routinator is still running its first validation. That is not an error: RAVEN retries with a growing delay (retry_in is in nanoseconds) and holds route annotation until the cache has data.

Once Routinator has data, RAVEN logs RTR session established, then RTR sync complete with the cache's vrp_count and aspa_count, then RTR ready — starting route annotation. If aspa_count stays 0, see ASPA Validation Not Working.

docs.title: Step 3 — Configure Your Router
docs.text:
Point your router's BMP configuration at RAVEN's BMP listener.

FRR example: router bgp 65000 bmp targets raven address 192.0.2.10 port 11019 monitor ipv4 unicast pre-policy monitor ipv6 unicast pre-policy exit exit

SR Linux example: network-instance default { protocols { bgp { bmp { station raven { connection { destination-address 192.0.2.10 destination-port 11019 } local-address 0.0.0.0 } } } } }

docs.title: Step 4 — Check Peer Status
docs.text:
Once your router connects:

raven status

RAVEN dev  uptime 4m12s

Route Table: 1160117 routes received (Adj-RIB-In pre-policy)
  origin-only          601877
  unverified           540112
  secured              10214
  origin-invalid       6872
  path-only            742
  path-suspect         300

RPKI: 786344 VRPs (serial 4821)

BMP Peers: 2
  ROUTER  PEER          ASN    STATE  ROUTES
  edge1   198.51.100.1  64496  up     948213
  edge1   2001:db8::1   64496  up     211904

Each row under BMP Peers is one BGP session on your router, which BMP reports as a peer. ROUTER is the router's BMP sysName and ROUTES is what that peer sent before your import policy. If ROUTES is still climbing, the router is sending its initial table dump; wait for it to settle before you query routes. A RPKI: line with 0 VRPs means RAVEN has not completed a sync with your validator yet. See raven status for every column.

docs.title: Step 5 — Query Your Routes
docs.text:
# Show all routes with their security posture
raven routes

# Show only routes failing ROV
raven routes --posture origin-invalid

# Show routes with ASPA path violations
raven routes --posture path-suspect

# Show routes for a specific prefix
raven routes --prefix 1.0.0.0/24

docs.title: Step 6 — Watch for Problems in Real Time
docs.text:
raven watch --posture origin-invalid

This streams any new origin-invalid routes to your terminal as they arrive. Leave it running — it will catch hijacks and ROV state changes as they happen.

docs.title: Step 7 — Run a What-If Simulation
docs.text:
raven what-if --reject-invalid

This shows you how many routes would be dropped if you deployed reject-invalid policy today — without changing anything on your routers.

docs.title: Demo Lab Overview
docs.text: RAVEN ships with a complete Containerlab topology that runs the full routing security stack on your laptop. This is the same lab used for conference demos.

docs.title: What the Lab Gives You
docs.text:
• Four FRR routers simulating a real network topology (including an attacker node)
  • Live BGP sessions with BMP streaming to RAVEN
  • Routinator serving real RPKI data including ASPA objects
  • Prometheus and Grafana with pre-built dashboards
  • Scripted attack scenarios — IPv4/IPv6 origin hijack, route leak (ASPA), what-if simulation

docs.title: Topology
docs.text:
The lab topology consists of four FRR routers and RAVEN connected via Containerlab: 

                Internet (AS64496)
                       │ eBGP
                       ▼
        Upstream (AS65000) ─── eBGP ─── Attacker (AS65099)
                       │ eBGP                           │ eBGP
                       ▼                                │
                Edge (AS65001) ──────────────────────────┘
                       │ BMP (pre-policy)
                       ▼
                     RAVEN ◄── RTR ── Routinator
                       │
                       ▼
              Prometheus + Grafana

Node ASN Role internet AS64496 Originates 2001:db8:2121::/48 (IPv6 demo prefix); used as the IPv4 origin-hijack source for 192.0.2.0/24 upstream AS65000 Transit provider, sends post-policy BMP to RAVEN edge AS65001 Edge router, sends pre-policy BMP to RAVEN attacker AS65099 Peered with upstream and edge; used for stealthy hijack and IPv6 origin hijack

AS64496 is from RFC 5398's documentation/private range — chosen so the lab never collides with real-world RPKI records. The route-leak scenario uses real-world RPKI data: upstream (AS65000) re-originates 145.102.136.0/22 (owned by AS1199 / SURFnet, with a real ROA) and prepends AS1199 in the AS_PATH. AS1199's published ASPA lists AS1103 as its only authorized provider, so the hop AS1199→AS65000 fires ASPA:Invalid and the route lands in path-suspect.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Containerlab — install guide
  • Docker — running and accessible without sudo (or use sudo)
  • Routinator — native binary or Docker (see Installing Routinator below)
  • RAVEN — built from source or installed via go install
  • Prometheus — Docker container
  • Grafana — Docker container

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
A Docker image is available at nlnetlabs/routinator:latest. Save the following as ~/.routinator.conf:

repository-dir = "/home/routinator/.rpki-cache/repository"
rtr-listen = ["0.0.0.0:3323"]
http-listen = ["0.0.0.0:8323"]
disable-rsync = true
enable-aspa = true

Then start the container:

docker run -d --name routinator \
  -p 3323:3323 \
  -v ~/.routinator.conf:/home/routinator/.routinator.conf:ro \
  -v ~/.rpki-cache:/home/routinator/.rpki-cache \
  nlnetlabs/routinator:latest \
  server

docs.title: Native Binary
docs.text:
# Install via cargo
cargo install routinator

# Or download a pre-built binary from
# https://github.com/NLnetLabs/routinator/releases

# Create config
mkdir -p ~/.rpki-cache/repository
cat > ~/.routinator.conf << 'CONF'
repository-dir = "/home/YOUR_USER/.rpki-cache/repository"
rtr-listen = ["127.0.0.1:3323"]
http-listen = ["127.0.0.1:8323"]
disable-rsync = true
CONF

# Start Routinator (first run takes ~4 minutes to sync)
routinator server &

Warning

Routinator takes approximately 4 minutes for a cold start while it downloads and validates the RPKI repository. A warm cache restart takes about 13 seconds. Do not kill Routinator between demos — the warm cache is essential for reliable demo startup.

docs.title: Quick Lab Start
docs.text:
From the RAVEN repository root:

bash lab/demo-master.sh setup

This command:

  1. Deploys the Containerlab topology
  2. Waits for FRR BGP sessions to converge
  3. Verifies Routinator is running and synced
  4. Starts RAVEN
  5. Starts Prometheus and Grafana
  6. Imports the Grafana dashboard
  7. Runs a baseline check

The script reports each step as it goes; ✓ Routinator RTR ready confirms that Routinator is serving validated data. It then prints the route table (raven routes) and finishes with these lines, which are fixed text in demo-master.sh:

✓ Setup complete.

  Grafana:    http://localhost:3000/d/raven-security-posture  (admin / raven123)
  Prometheus: http://localhost:9090
  RAVEN API:  http://localhost:11020
  Metrics:    http://localhost:9595/metrics

  Expected postures (baseline — 5 routes, path-suspect = 0):
    origin-only    → 100.64.0.0/24, 198.51.100.0/24, 203.0.113.0/24, 10.10.0.0/24
    unverified     → 10.99.99.0/24
    path-suspect   → (none at baseline)

To see RAVEN's own view of the RPKI data, check the RPKI: line of raven status, or the raven_rtr_vrp_count and raven_rtr_aspa_count metrics.
